card.name: Harul
card.tagline: A narrative folk dance of the Jaunsari and Hatee tribes in the Himalayan foothills.
card.profile: Harul is a traditional folk song-and-dance practice performed by the Jaunsari tribe of Uttarakhand and the Hatee tribe of Himachal Pradesh. The dance serves as a living narrative, with participants recounting heroic tales of gods, goddesses, and tribal history through song. Performed in long lines or semi-circles, the dance emphasizes communal connection and rhythmic footwork. It is a central feature of local festivals and celebrations in the Jaunsar-Bawar and Trans-Giri regions.
card.insight: In the high hills of Sirmaur, dancers link hands in long, shifting chains to recite the history of their gods through the rhythmic, criss-crossing movement of their feet.

card.profile_long: The Harul dance is a foundational cultural expression for the Jaunsari tribe in Uttarakhand and the Hatee tribe in Himachal Pradesh. It is not merely a performance but a vessel for the oral history of these communities, functioning as a song-cum-dance tradition that preserves the heroic stories of regional deities and significant historical events. The dance is deeply embedded in the social fabric of the Jaunsar-Bawar and Trans-Giri regions of the Sirmaur district, where it is performed during local festivals and celebrations. The structure of the dance is inherently communal, requiring participants to hold onto one another to form a singular, cohesive unit. This formation, typically a long line, allows the dancers to move in unison, reflecting the shared history they are reciting. In some instances, the participants organize themselves into semi-circles, with a distinct gender-based arrangement where men form the outer semi-circle and women form the inner one. Those at the ends of the line hold up with a single hand, maintaining the tension and continuity of the chain. The physical movement of Harul is characterized by a blend of slow and fast footwork, which includes tapping and criss-crossing steps as the dancers move across the space. These movements are punctuated by occasional knee bending, all performed in strict synchronization with the rhythm of the accompanying song. The songs themselves are narrative in nature, often structured as a conversation between a man and a woman, which dictates the flow and tempo of the dance. Participants wear traditional, colourful clothing that adds to the visual vibrancy of the performance. The mood of the dance is consistently cheerful, reflecting its role in community celebrations. Because the dance relies on the narrative content of the song, the movement is inextricably linked to the vocal performance. The dancers must remain attentive to the shifts in the narrative, as the footwork and rhythm adapt to the unfolding story. This tradition remains a living practice, passed down through the generations as a way to maintain the cultural identity of the Jaunsari and Hatee people. The dance requires no complex stagecraft, relying instead on the collective movement of the participants and the power of the oral tradition. It is a testament to the endurance of the tribal cultures in the Himalayan foothills, where the history of the land is kept alive through the rhythmic tapping of feet and the shared voices of the community. The dance is not restricted to a specific age group, allowing for a broad participation that reinforces the communal spirit of the tribes. As the dancers move, they are not just performing steps but are actively participating in the transmission of their cultural heritage, ensuring that the tales of the past remain relevant in the present day.

sections.origins_and_history: Harul originates from the Jaunsari tribe of Uttarakhand and the Hatee tribe of Himachal Pradesh. It is specifically associated with the Jaunsar-Bawar and Trans-Giri regions of the Sirmaur district.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Participants form long lines or semi-circles, holding onto each other. Men typically form the outer semi-circle and women the inner. The footwork involves slow and fast tapping, criss-crossing, and occasional knee bending in rhythm with the song.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music consists of narrative songs that recount the history and heroic tales of gods and goddesses. These songs often feature a conversational format between a man and a woman.
sections.costume_and_setting: Participants wear colourful traditional clothing. The dance is performed in the context of local festivals and celebrations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Harul is performed during local festivals and celebrations, serving as a medium to share the history and mythology of the Jaunsari and Hatee tribes.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is performed in both the Jaunsar-Bawar region of Uttarakhand and the Trans-Giri region of Sirmaur district in Himachal Pradesh.
sections.lineage: Shares similarities with the Nati dance.

claims.text: Harul is a special form of folk song and dance performed by the Jaunsari tribe in Uttarakhand and the Hatee tribe in Himachal Pradesh.
Participants hold on to each other to form a long line or semi-circles.
The participants may organize themselves into semi-circles, with men forming the outer circle and women the inner.
The dance involves slow and fast footwork, tapping, and criss-crossing.
The songs are narrative and often feature a conversation between a man and a woman.
Harul is significant in local festivals and celebrations.
